3.text: away from it. The greater part of the people moved inland in order to attack the enemy from

4.text: behind. Some few went directly to the village under cover of the fog. One old man said, ‘Give

5.text: voice, like wolves howling.’ They howled like wolves. Then among the St. Lawrence people

6.text: another old man started, and said, ‘Oh, they are here!’ The younger people answered, ‘Is it pos-

7.text: sible? But we are on an island.’ — ‘Oh, yes! Give answer, you also.’ Then they roared like

8.text: walrus. Meanwhile the larger troop of assailants, those that were behind, were slowly approaching.

9.text: All of a sudden they attacked the islanders, and began to kill them. The women, from sheer fright,

10.text: strangled themselves. Others carved walrus-meat, with which to treat the victors. A great slaughter

11.text: ensued. Numerous women were taken prisoners and carried to Indian Point.

12.text: “After four years the St. Lawrence people, in their turn, sought revenge. They came in the

13.text: night-time, and succeeded in surprising the people in their sleep. They killed them simply by

14.text: thrusting their spears through the skin walls of the sleeping-room. One small orphan-boy, however,

15.text: fled in time, and wakened the people. Then the assailants fled to the open sea. The next year

16.text: the old men of St. Lawrence said, ‘It is enough. Let all the people make peace among themselves.’

17.text: The summer came, and a number of the islanders came to the shore. They brought a large num-

18.text: ber of wooden vessels, and gave them to the people of this land. An old man of our shore said,

19.text: ‘How will you answer them? Give them skins.’ They gave them soft skins. ‘What skins are

20.text: these?’ — ‘Reindeer-skins!’ — ‘What is a reindeer?’ — ‘They are with antlers!’ — ‘What are

21.text: antlers?’ So they showed them a part of some skin from the head of a reindeer. They looked at

22.text: it, and said, ‘Oh, how wonderful! The nose is like the holes in the hide cover of a boat.’ — ‘You

23.text: had better try the meat!’ They cooked some reindeer-fat. — ‘Oh, well! it is like blubber.’ Then

24.text: they ate of it. ‘Oh, it tastes good!’ They went away and left one man. He was a shaman; and

25.text: the people of this shore made him a prisoner in the same way as the islanders did four years ago

27.text: This is a very typical description of a war between two Maritime people

28.text: living on opposite shores of Bering Sea.

29.text: Tungus and Yukaghir Wars. — Chukchee intercourse with the Tungus

30.text: is quite recent, and almost nothing of it is reflected in the folk-stories. One

31.text: or two tales relating to it are quite short, and poor in details. The tales of

32.text: the eastern Tungus, on the contrary, contain a number of details about the

33.text: coming of the Chukchee and their struggle with the Tungus inhabitants of

34.text: the land. As to the Yukaghir, the Chukchee tales hardly mention them.

35.text: Yukaghir tradition, on the contrary, asserts that the Chukchee and the Yukaghir

36.text: were friendly among themselves; and one time, when a certain Chukchee was

37.text: killed unintentially by the Yukaghir, and they saw his face, they exclaimed with

38.text: much sorrow, “Sun, look on, we have killed a brother.”¹ But the Chukchee

39.text: tales contain nothing about the Veˊemɪlɪt (“river-settlers”), the name used for
